result: In wildtype neuromasts, each afferent neuron selectively innervates either all Emx2-positive or all Emx2-negative hair cells, establishing a correlation between Emx2 expression and neuronal selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 collectively demonstrate through immunostaining and single-neuron labeling that wildtype afferent neurons segregate based on Emx2 expression in HCs. The data in Figure 1 provides clear visual evidence of this selective innervation pattern, with neurons associating exclusively with either Emx2-positive or Emx2-negative HCs.

result: In emx2 knockout and gain-of-function mutants where all HCs are unidirectionally oriented, afferent neurons show altered branching patterns with two distinct populations: major neurons innervating ~70% of HCs and minor neurons innervating ~20% of HCs, compared to the consistent ~50% in wildtype.
evaluation: Claims C33-C41 are well-supported by quantitative data in Figure 2 showing statistically significant differences (p<0.01) in innervation overlap between wildtype and both emx2 mutants. The segregation into major and minor populations is clearly demonstrated with appropriate controls and statistical analysis.

result: Quantitative analysis of HC contacts reveals that in emx2 mutants, major afferent neurons contact significantly more HCs (74.8-75.2%) while minor neurons contact significantly fewer HCs (25.4-25.8%) compared to wildtype (52.9%), with nerve endings properly juxtaposed to HC bodies in all cases.
evaluation: Claims C42-C48 are strongly supported by detailed quantitative data in Figure 3 and Table 1, with highly significant p-values (p<1E-18 to 1E-25). The anatomical evidence shows proper nerve ending positioning in mutants, and the 3:2 ratio of major to minor neurons is documented. Sample sizes are adequate (n=11-26 neuromasts).

result: Both major and minor afferent neurons in emx2 mutants associate with presynaptic RibeyeB puncta, though incomplete synapses (nerve endings adjacent to but not directly associated with presynapses) are more prevalent in mutants, particularly in minor fibers.
evaluation: Claims C49-C55 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4 with appropriate quantification. The decrease in RibeyeB-nerve ending colocalization is statistically significant for minor fibers (p<0.01) but not major fibers. Mander's colocalization coefficients provide additional quantitative support, though the significance is marginal for some comparisons.

result: While the number of complete synapses per HC (RibeyeB-Maguk colocalization) is similar between wildtype and emx2 mutants, there is a significant increase in solitary (uncoupled) pre- and post-synaptic puncta in mutants, indicating failures in synapse formation.
evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are well-supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 5 with strong statistical significance (p<1E-07 for most comparisons). The data clearly show increased uncoupling of synaptic components despite similar complete synapse numbers. Sample sizes are adequate (n=18-25 neuromasts from three independent experiments).

result: Calcium imaging reveals that afferent neurons in emx2 mutants are functional and directionally selective, responding only to stimuli matching their HC orientation. Mutant afferents show increased total calcium signals (41-58% higher) due to recruiting additional HCs, but per-HC signal magnitude remains unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C62-C73 are strongly supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 6 with appropriate statistical analysis. The directional selectivity is clearly demonstrated, and the increased total signal with unchanged per-HC signal provides mechanistic insight. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-13 neuromasts) with significant p-values where claimed.

result: Electrophysiological recordings confirm that afferent neurons in emx2 mutants fire action potentials in a directionally selective manner matching their HC orientation, with dramatically reduced responses to off-stimulus directions, and spike numbers in the on-stimulus direction not exceeding wildtype.
evaluation: Claims C74-C80 are supported by extracellular recording data in Figure 7. The complete segregation of neuron types in mutants (8/8 P>A in ko, 7/7 A>P in gof) is striking. Statistical comparisons show no significant difference in on-stimulus spike numbers (p>0.6), supporting the interpretation. This complements the calcium imaging data.

result: In vangl2m209 mutants with randomly oriented hair bundles, Emx2 expression remains in 50% of HCs and afferent neurons still selectively innervate based on Emx2 status, demonstrating that neuronal selectivity is independent of hair bundle orientation and directed by Emx2. Genetic epistasis analysis shows vangl2 is epistatic to emx2 for hair bundle orientation.
evaluation: Claims C81-C91, C106-C107, C117-C118 are well-supported by data in Figure 8. The maintenance of 50% Emx2-positive HCs (p=0.67) and similar innervation ratios (p=0.26) in vangl2 mutants despite random hair bundle orientation provides strong evidence for independence of these processes. The epistasis analysis with double mutants is appropriately conducted and interpreted.

result: Emx2 regulates directional selectivity of neuromasts through two distinct processes: controlling hair bundle orientation in HCs and directing selective afferent neuronal innervation patterns, thereby preserving directional information at both the sensory and neural levels.
evaluation: Claims C5, C8-C11, C114-C115 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the collective evidence from anatomical, functional, and genetic experiments. The dual role of Emx2 is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches with consistent results across different experimental paradigms.

result: In emx2 mutants, neurons demonstrate capacity to innervate additional HCs of similar orientation based on availability, but there is an upper limit to this capacity as single neurons cannot innervate all HCs within a mutant neuromast.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by the quantitative data showing major neurons innervate ~75% (not 100%) of HCs in mutants. This interpretation is reasonable given the consistent observation that no single neuron innervates all available HCs, suggesting intrinsic limitations to innervation capacity.

result: Despite increased post-synaptic calcium signals in the entire afferent terminal of emx2 mutants, this increase does not translate into more evoked spikes at the single afferent neuron level.
evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by comparing calcium imaging (Figure 6) and electrophysiology (Figure 7) data. The apparent paradox is acknowledged by the authors with discussion of potential explanations including insufficient signal increase, variability in recordings, and heterogeneous neuron populations.

result: Emx2 and Vangl2 are independently regulated proteins, with Emx2 controlling both hair bundle orientation and neuronal innervation while Vangl2 only regulates hair bundle orientation. However, vangl2 is epistatic to emx2 for hair bundle orientation, consistent with Vangl2 functioning intercellularly to regulate intracellular Emx2 signaling.
evaluation: Claims C108-C112 are supported by the vangl2 mutant analysis and genetic epistasis experiments. The independence is demonstrated by maintained Emx2 expression in vangl2 mutants and cited evidence of maintained Vangl2 in Emx2 ko mice. The epistasis relationship is clearly shown by double mutant phenotypes resembling vangl2 single mutants.

result: Neurons innervating Emx2-positive versus Emx2-negative HCs may be molecularly distinct populations, analogous to mammalian vestibular neurons. The selective innervation may require molecular matching between HCs and neurons, with additional permissive factors beyond Emx2 that can allow innervation expansion under certain conditions.
evaluation: Claims C95-C101 represent speculative discussion points based on analogy to other systems and interpretation of axotomy studies. While the reasoning is logical and the cited evidence (C95, C97, C99-C100) is appropriate, these claims are not directly tested in the current study. The 'inclusive model' remains a hypothesis requiring future experimental validation.

result: Given the conserved role of Emx2 in mechanosensory organs, its function in regulating post-synaptic partner selection may extend to other neural systems where Emx2 is expressed, such as cortex and olfactory epithelium.
evaluation: Claim C116 is speculative extrapolation beyond the data presented. While the reasoning is logical given Emx2's conserved role in hair bundle orientation and its expression in other neural tissues, this hypothesis requires direct experimental testing in those systems.

result: The lateral line system consists of neuromasts with bidirectionally oriented hair bundles that detect water flow direction, with each afferent neuron innervating only HCs of the same orientation, independent of HC activity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C12-C22 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from previous literature. These foundational concepts are well-accepted in the field and provide necessary context for the current study.

result: Emx2 is expressed in half of the HCs within a neuromast (one daughter cell from each HC precursor division) and functions to reverse hair bundle orientation by approximately 180 degrees from the default state, enabling detection of water flow from opposite directions.
evaluation: Claims C4, C24-C27, C113 summarize previous work by the authors (Jiang et al., 2017) that established Emx2's role in hair bundle orientation. This prior work is appropriately cited and provides the foundation for investigating Emx2's role in neuronal selectivity.

result: The molecular mechanisms determining how directional selectivity is preserved at the level of neuronal innervation were unknown prior to this study.
evaluation: Claim C23 accurately identifies the knowledge gap that motivated this study. This is supported by the literature review showing that while activity-independent selection was established, molecular mechanisms remained unclear.

result: In emx2 knockout neuromasts all HCs are oriented P>A and neurons respond only to P>A stimulation; in emx2 gain-of-function neuromasts all HCs are oriented A>P and neurons respond only to A>P stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C103-C104 are supported by both anatomical data (Figures 2-3) showing unidirectional HC orientation and functional data (Figures 6-7) showing directionally selective responses matching HC orientation. This demonstrates the predicted relationship between HC orientation and neuronal responses.
